n: About twenty years into his reign, Solomon has completed both the temple and his own palace complex. The narrator pauses at this high point, just before the Lord speaks to him again.
This is Solomon’s second recorded revelation. The first came at Gibeon, where he asked for an understanding heart. Now the Lord answers the dedicatory prayer he offered in chapter 8.
The Lord accepts the temple. To “put my name there” means the house belongs to Him and represents His presence among His people; His eyes and heart being there promises ongoing, personal attention.

f.g: made holy; set apart for sacred use.

n: The blessing is conditional. Solomon is invited to walk as David did—with integrity, a whole and undivided heart—and to keep all the Lord’s laws.

f.g: Hebrew tom-levav: wholeness or completeness of heart, not perfection without flaw.

n: If Solomon is faithful, the Lord will keep His promise to David that a descendant would always sit on Israel’s throne.

f.w: There shall not fail thee a man

n: The warning now shifts to “ye”—plural. It covers Solomon and all his descendants: turning to other gods would break the covenant.

The consequence of apostasy would be exile and the loss of the temple’s sacred status. Israel would become a “byword,” a cautionary tale people mention with scorn. This was fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests.

f.g: a saying used to mock; Israel’s fate would become a cautionary example.

n: Even the temple, high and glorious, would become a ruin that shocks passersby. “Hiss” describes a whistle of astonishment or contempt in the ancient world.

f.g: to whistle in amazement or scorn at a ruin.

n: The answer to the onlookers’ question is the lesson of the whole book of Kings: Israel’s disasters came because they forsook the God who freed them from Egypt.

f.g: here, calamity or disaster, not moral wickedness.

n: The narrative turns from revelation to administration. Seven years for the temple and thirteen for the palace make twenty years of building.
Hiram of Tyre, a Phoenician king, had supplied timber and gold. In payment, Solomon handed over twenty towns in Galilee, near the border with Tyre.
Hiram travels to inspect the towns and is unimpressed—a hint that Solomon may have given him poor land.
Hiram’s nickname for the region, “Cabul,” likely sounded like “good for nothing.” Calling Solomon “my brother” is the normal language of treaty partners.

f.g: possibly a wordplay meaning ‘as nothing’ or ‘worthless’; also the name of a town in Asher (Joshua 19:27).
a diplomatic term for an allied king of equal rank.

n: Hiram nonetheless sends a huge sum of gold—roughly four tons. The exchange shows the close commercial ties between the two kingdoms.

f.g: 120 talents; a talent weighed roughly 75 pounds (34 kg).

n: The “levy” was forced labor. Solomon used it for the temple, palace, Jerusalem’s fortifications, and three key fortress cities guarding major trade routes.

f.g: probably earthen terraces or fill supporting buildings in Jerusalem; the word means ‘filling.’

n: An aside explains how Gezer came into Solomon’s hands: Pharaoh conquered it and gave it as a dowry when his daughter married Solomon.
Solomon rebuilt Gezer and Lower Beth-horon, which guarded the main road climbing from the coast to Jerusalem.
Baalath and Tadmor were outposts. Tadmor is often linked with Palmyra in the Syrian desert, though some manuscripts read Tamar, a town in southern Judah.
Solomon built storage cities for supplies and bases for his chariot forces. His building projects stretched all through his realm.
These are the remnants of the Canaanite peoples who lived in the land before Israel.

f.w: Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites

n: Since Israel never fully drove these peoples out, Solomon made them a permanent labor force. The phrase “unto this day” shows the writer is looking back from a later time.

f.g: permanent forced labor, harder than the temporary levy on Israelites.

n: Israelites were not made permanent slaves; they served instead as soldiers, officials, and commanders. (Israelites did, however, serve in rotating labor crews, 1 Kings 5:13.)
Solomon’s administration included 550 supervisors over the work crews—a picture of a large, organized state.
Pharaoh’s daughter moved from the old city of David into her own palace. Only then did Solomon build the Millo.
Solomon personally led worship at the three great annual feasts—Passover, Pentecost (Weeks), and Tabernacles—fulfilling the law’s pattern.

f.g: sacrifices shared in a fellowship meal, celebrating peace with God.

n: Solomon built a fleet at Ezion-geber near modern Eilat on the Gulf of Aqaba, giving Israel access to Red Sea trade.
Phoenicians were the expert seafarers of the age, so Hiram supplied experienced sailors to crew the ships alongside Solomon’s men.
The fleet returned from Ophir with about sixteen tons of gold. Ophir’s location is uncertain—suggestions include Arabia, East Africa, or India—but it became a byword for fine gold.
